podcast.title: R.E.M.'s Multinational Era (Post-1987)
podcast.body: R.E.M. transitioned to Warner Music after experiencing "problems and certain disagreements" with their previous independent label, IRS Records, around 1987. From this point forward, R.E.M. consistently remained with multinational labels, releasing what many consider their "great trilogy" of albums, which are revered as some of the finest in US music history. "se pasaría a Warner y a partir de ahí rem estaría siempre multinacionales."

podcast.title: Red Hot Chili Peppers' New Label (1991)
podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers moved to Warner Records from EMI for the release of their pivotal album "Blood Sugar Sex Magik" in 1991. "First of all, the Chili Peppers switch labels moving from EMI to Warner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Green Day's Dookie Release (1994)
podcast.body: Warner released Green Day's *Dookie* album (referred to as "Ducky album" in the transcript) in February 1994, after being tipped off to the band's initial two releases on the indie label Lookout Records. "in February 1994, Warner released Green Day's Ducky album after being tipped off to the band's first two releases on an indie called Lookout Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dropping 5440 from US Deal (c. 1995)
podcast.body: Warner dropped 5440 from their American record deal around 1995, following the release of the band's sixth record, "Smiling Buddha Cabaret." This decision plunged 5440 into an "existential moment" as they considered their future without a major American label. "They were dropped by a Warner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Acquisition of Catalogs
podcast.body: Warner's publishing arm is actively scooping up music catalogs, often from artists who have been signed to them for many years. "Then you add in the publishing arms of labels like Universal and Sony and Warner, who were also scooping up catalogues, usually of artists who have been their signings for years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Videoclip Promotion
podcast.body: In the 1970s, the program "Pop Clips" in the United States began programming videoclips from the Warner catalog as a strategy to promote their artists. "El estado sonido, en los años 70, hace pop clips, se ocó a la empezo a programar videoclips levantas del catalogo de la Warner para promocionar a sus artistas."

podcast.title: Major Label Status
podcast.body: Warner is identified as one of the four multinational giants in the music industry, responsible for a large share of recorded music distribution worldwide. It, too, operates with its own array of subsidiary labels. "Universal, EMI, Sony BMG, and Warner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major Label Status and Location
podcast.body: Warner is one of the three major multinational record corporations. Its operations are run out of New York. "Warner, which is run out of New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major Record Label
podcast.body: Warner is identified as one of the three major record labels that dominate the music industry, operating as a multinational entity controlling a significant portion of the world's music trade and revenue. "The music industry is dominated by three major record labels, Universal, Sony, and Warner."

podcast.title: MusicNet (Failed Online Music Store)
podcast.body: Warner was one of the labels involved with "MusicNet," an early online music store created by major labels in an attempt to sell digital files. Similar to its competitor, this service was difficult to use, featured restrictions, and was loaded with complicated digital rights management (DRM) safeguards. It hung on longer than its competitor but was eventually sold off for parts in 2005. "MusicNet, which handled BMG, EMI and Warner."

podcast.body: Warner Music is identified as one of the three major recorded music companies. "their number has been whittled down to just three companies, the Universal, the biggest, Sony and Warner music."

podcast.title: One of Three Major Labels (Present Day)
podcast.body: Warner is identified as one of the three major multinational record labels in the present day, alongside Universal and Sony. It encompasses numerous subsidiary labels. "Today, we're down to just three. Universal, Sony and Warner and all their subsidiary labels, and there were dozens and dozens of those."

podcast.title: Parent Company of Atlantic Records
podcast.body: Warner was the parent company of Atlantic Records, which signed the band that founded Epitaph Records (Bad Religion) in late 1993. "Atlantic Records, who were part of Warner."

podcast.title: Release of 5440's Greatest Hits (Post-Drop)
podcast.body: Despite dropping 5440 from their US deal, Warner Canada later released a "Greatest Hits" album for the band. This compilation performed very well, providing significant "mailbox cash" for 5440 and helping to "reset" the band's reputation with the Canadian audience, giving MuchMusic more material to feature. "Warner Canada did that. Yeah. Which did really well. So bucket loads."

podcast.title: Role in Grooveshark's Closure
podcast.body: Warner Music, in collaboration with Universal Music and in response to Robert Fripp's complaints, launched a substantial attack against Grooveshark. This collective action was a pivotal factor in the platform's eventual shutdown. "Universal Music guarda el music atacan masivamente a Groofshark y acaban consiguiendo el cierre de la plataforma."

podcast.title: Staggered Crossing's Record Deal
podcast.body: The Toronto band Staggered Crossing secured a record deal with Warner Music in 1997, leading to the release of their debut album in 2001. "It's got a deal with Warner Music in 1997 and released a debut album in 2001."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vevo Joint Venture Partner
podcast.body: Warner was among the four major record labels that partnered to launch Vevo on December 8, 2009. This joint venture sought to establish a premier platform for music videos, providing a controlled environment for content distribution and advertising revenue generation. "Vivo, a joint venture between the four major record labels at the time, Universal, Sony, Warner and EMI."
